title: US midterms set to reshape Congress, test Trump and 2028 race
text:
US midterms set to reshape Congress, test Trump and 2028 race - CHOSUNBIZ 
 2026년 11월 4일(수) Industry Finance Real Estate IT Retail Science Policy Society International Entertainment Culture Sports English International US midterms set to reshape Congress, test Trump and 2028 race 
 Key races, turnout and legal fights could decide control of Congress and shape 2028 strategies 
 입력 2026.11.03. 11:39 업데이트   2026.11.03. 12:01 조선비즈 구글 검색 먼저 보기 With the U.S. midterm elections a day away, attention is focusing on key variables that will determine the balance of power in Congress. Forecasts largely expect the Democratic Party to regain the House majority, but some observers say the party is locked in a tight race with the Republican Party in the Senate. In particular, the outcome is likely to have a considerable impact on the remainder of U.S. President Donald Trump's term in office.
 A poster urging voting in the midterm elections set for the 3rd is posted on a wall in Dallas, Texas, United States. /Courtesy of AFP On the 2nd (local time), Reuters named six key things to watch in the U.S. midterm elections to be held on the 3rd. The six factors are the outlook in competitive House and Senate races, the potential for disputes in the voting and counting process, whether President Trump will accept the results, voter turnout, the impact on the 2028 presidential election, and the Republican Party's advantage in campaign funds.
 ◇ Congressional control hinges on swing-state wins and losses 
 In this election, all 435 House seats and some Senate seats are up for grabs. The Republican Party currently holds 218 seats in the House and 53 in the Senate, maintaining majorities in both chambers. For the Democratic Party to become the majority, it needs to pick up four more seats in each chamber.
 In the House, observers see a high likelihood of a Democratic victory. The Senate majority, by contrast, is expected to be decided by outcomes in six to eight competitive races. The Democrats need to flip Republican seats in Ohio and Iowa, Alaska, and Texas, where President Trump won the 2024 presidential election by double-digit margins. Kansas, where Trump won by 16 percentage points at the time, has also tightened into a close race recently.
 The Democrats can raise their chances of retaking the Senate majority if they hold the Michigan seat and win in Maine. Conversely, the Republicans can keep their Senate majority if they win in most of the key battlegrounds.
 Potential disputes in the voting and counting process are also a point of interest. The U.S. Department of Justice plans to deploy about 1,000 monitors nationwide on Election Day. That is roughly three times the previous midterms. Some local election officials worry that voters could feel intimidated, but the department denies this.
 In particular, the Department of Justice on the 22nd of last month filed a lawsuit seeking to block certification of the results if the Republican incumbent narrowly loses Alaska's Senate race. The reason cited was that two candidates with nearly identical names on the ballot could confuse voters. However, on the 1st, a federal court rejected the department's request, and the department appealed.
 Whether President Trump will accept the election results is also drawing attention. Since losing the 2020 presidential election, Trump has continued to claim fraud. In these midterms, he is also raising doubts about fairness. If the Republican Party loses its congressional majority, some worry that conflicts over the results could intensify.
 United States President Donald Trump. The photo shows him delivering a speech at a midterm campaign rally in Dubuque, Iowa, on the 1st. /Courtesy of Reuters ◇ Next presidential strategies will shift with voter sentiment 
 Turnout among the parties' bases is critical. Polls show Democratic supporters more eager to vote than Republican supporters, but young people and Black and Hispanic voters—key Democratic constituencies—have historically turned out at lower rates in midterms than in presidential elections.
 If their actual participation falls short of expectations, the scale of a Democratic victory could shrink. In some states, early voting saw strong participation from Democratic supporters, but the Republican Party expects many of its voters to cast ballots on Election Day.
 Another focus is how the Republican Party's advantage in campaign funds actually influenced voters. Counting party organizations and outside groups, Republicans spent hundreds of millions of dollars more than Democrats. According to Federal Election Commission (FEC) data, more than $277 million (about 372.1 billion won) flowed through independent expenditure political action committees (super PACs) supporting President Trump, including "MAGA Inc.," to fund late-campaign TV ads and mailers backing Republican candidates. Tesla Chief Executive Officer Elon Musk also spent about $366 million (about 491.6 billion won) supporting Republican candidates during this midterm period. Of that, $276 million (about 370.7 billion won) was spent since July.
 The impact of these elections on the 2028 presidential race is another area of interest. Within the Democratic Party, arguments to emphasize voter-friendly economic policies are clashing with calls to target the center. Depending on which faction's candidates perform well in this election, strategies for the next presidential race are likely to shift.
 If the Republican Party retains its congressional majority, President Trump could gain momentum for his policy agenda. If the Democrats seize the Senate or House, Congress could expand investigations into immigration enforcement, the Iran war, and ethics issues in the administration. The outcome is expected to affect not only the remainder of Trump's term but also the balance of power in U.S. politics heading into the next presidential election.
